subject: designs:  generated model concept + template code org

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: designs:  generated model concept + template code org
parts:
I'm driving toward the model concept (in the C++ sense)
described here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

The main differences from what we have now are:

1. no more virtual functions, no more log_prob_grad
intermediate base class; I'll probably get rid
of the log_prob base class. All classes and functions
using models now have a template parameter for the
model class.

2. templated methods for log prob with
a template param to suppress the Jacobian adjust
for transformed params (suggestions for the param name
would be appreciated --- it's now jacobian_adjust_transforms).

3. only a minimal set of functions remain, with other
functionality pulled out into statics that take the model
class as a template parameter and the model as an argument.

There's no overall loss in functionality.

One advantage of pulling out the utilities into statics
is that conceptually at least, the generated model class
without the main only depends on std::vector and stan::math
(and any probability function used).

If we can organize the necessary template code for
VectorView and OperandsAndPartials, we should also be able
to have a probability lib that doesn't depend on our
var or fvar.

I organized the new functor-based definition framework that way:

branch: feature/functor

Function definitions don't depend on var or fvar, and you only
pull in the metaprogramming libs for those types if you need them.
It's pretty easy to do this with argument-dependent lookup.

I'd like to get VectorView and OperandsAndPartials into the
same shape (and also renamed out of camel case!).
The specializations of these classes to var and fvar then
go in stan::agrad namespace and in their own files. The
result is a cleanly separated math lib and var and fvar
lib.

Even if nobody uses just the double-only versions, it seems
like a reasonable way to me to organize the code to minimize
dependencies. For instance, HMC doesn't need to bring in
fvar, so incompleteness in the fvar lib won't restrict usage
of HMC as it would if we just continue to pile in functions.

- Bob
